item.title: AI governance needs to consider users’ emotional responses
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02620-3

People will often trust or distrust an artificial intelligence (AI) output because of how it makes them feel, rather than how reliable it is. AI governance frameworks should require that platforms disclose design choices that target user emotions, allow users control over these, and include features aimed to calibrate trust.
item.dc:title: AI governance needs to consider users’ emotional responses
item.dc:creator: Daniel Västfjäll

item.title: Decredentialed jobs and upward mobility among non-college workers in the USA
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02610-5

Linking job postings to US Census earnings records from 2011 to 2021, Lyttelton et al. find that non-college workers hired into jobs that dropped degree requirements earned around US$4,600 more per year, yet employers rarely hired non-college workers after decredentialing.
item.dc:title: Decredentialed jobs and upward mobility among non-college workers in the USA
item.dc:creator: Thomas Lyttelton
Dylan K. Nelson
Nathan Wilmers

item.title: Within-family heritability estimates for behavioural and disease phenotypes from 500,000 sibling pairs of diverse ancestries
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02599-x

Using the variation in DNA sharing between 500,000 sibling pairs with diverse genetic ancestries, Yengo et al. estimate the heritability of 14 complex traits.

item.title: Generative AI and the temporary upskilling of knowledge workers
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02566-6

This randomized trial by Wiles et al. shows that generative AI helps knowledge workers perform data science tasks outside their skill set, but workers do not retain the underlying knowledge when the tool is removed.

item.title: Large language models for computational social science
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02539-9

This Review from Evans et al. documents the distinct roles that LLMs now have in computational social science and provides an overview of recent LLM-supported advances across fields including economics, psychology, political science, sociology and anthropology.
